claims.text: The initial W–Cu composite contains W particles or interconnected W ligaments embedded in a Cu matrix.
The initial composite exhibits W–Cu phase separation and interfacial voids.
Interfacial voids and phase separation impair thermal conduction, particularly under plasma-facing-joint service conditions.
A single HPHT consolidation treatment at approximately 3 GPa and 1373 K for one hour is proposed.
The proposed processing temperature is below the melting point of copper.
The proposed processing temperature is high enough to activate interfacial diffusion.
High pressure drives intimate contact between the W and Cu phases.
Elevated temperature facilitates interfacial diffusion between W and Cu.
HPHT treatment promotes densification and partial W–Cu interdiffusion at the interface.
HPHT treatment eliminates interfacial voids.
HPHT treatment reduces the interfacial free energy associated with phase separation.
Densification and interdiffusion produce a continuous, compositionally graded W–Cu interface.
The graded interface suppresses phase segregation and void nucleation.
Improved interfacial coherence and bonding reduce thermal interface resistance.
Reduced thermal interface resistance increases the composite's effective thermal conductivity.
The HPHT-treated composite is predicted to have more than 20% higher effective thermal conductivity than the untreated composite.
The predicted conductivity improvement will persist under both high-heat-flux and irradiation conditions.
The treatment is beneficial only when it promotes bonding without causing unwanted grain coarsening or deleterious phase transformations.
The treatment is limited to composites in which void formation is predominantly interfacial and service conditions remain within the stability limits of the densified interface.
The long-term stability of the HPHT-treated interface under extended irradiation is unconfirmed.

contradictions.description: The treatment is said to remain below copper's melting point, but the example temperature is 1373 K, slightly above the standard melting point of pure Cu (about 1358 K). Pressure-dependent melting behavior is not supplied to reconcile this discrepancy.
